titulo: DSTs – Sexually Transmitted Diseases and the Geopolitics of Health
pergunta: How do global policies to combat sexually transmitted diseases (DSTs) influence public health, the economy, and international relations, including in Brazil?
paraComecar:
Sexually transmitted diseases (DSTs), also called sexually transmitted infections (STIs), are illnesses transmitted mainly through vaginal, anal, or oral sex. Often they show no symptoms in the early stages, which facilitates silent transmission between partners and even from mother to child during pregnancy or birth.

There are more than 30 causative agents – bacteria (such as chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis), viruses (genital herpes, VIH/SIDA, human papillomavirus – VPH) and parasites (trichomoniasis). Some are curable (syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomoniasis) and others are treatable but not curable (herpes, hepatitis B, VIH/SIDA, VPH). Effective prevention includes abstinence, condom use, reducing the number of partners, and vaccines (for example, against hepatitis B and some types of VPH).

In 2015, about 1,1 bilhão people worldwide were infected with an STD other than VIH/SIDA; 500 milhões had syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia or trichomoniasis, 530 milhões had genital herpes and 290 milhões women were infected with VPH. These infections caused 108 mil deaths that year. In developed countries diagnostic tests are widely available, whereas in many developing nations they remain scarce, hampering epidemic control.

Beyond the direct health impact, DSTs generate economic costs (treatment, loss of productivity) and create social stigma that hinders seeking health services. Therefore, international bodies, governments and funding agencies develop joint policies – from sexual education campaigns to vaccine procurement agreements – that influence not only public health but also diplomatic and commercial relations between countries, including Brazil, which participates in global prevention and treatment initiatives.

numeros.valor:
International guidelines recommend safe‑sex practices – condom use, reducing the number of partners and monogamy – as the first line of prevention; sexual abstinence is pointed out as the most effective measure, although it is rarely adopted in public policies.

Specific vaccines, such as those against hepatitis B and certain types of HPV, are included in immunisation programmes to lower the incidence of infections that have no cure. Male circumcision is also cited as a preventive measure in some contexts.

Developed countries usually have widely available diagnostic tests, allowing early treatment and transmission control. In developing countries, the lack of these tests hampers the identification of asymptomatic cases, increasing the risk of spread.

National governments, together with international health organisations, set financing and resource‑distribution policies (vaccines, medicines, test kits). The cost of treatment and prevention is typically borne by public health systems or international assistance programmes, while antibiotic resistance in gonorrhoea demonstrates the need for constant updates to therapeutic guidelines.

Social stigma surrounding STIs, historically linked to shame and taboo, influences policy effectiveness: stigma can prevent people from seeking diagnosis and treatment, reducing the impact of public and international investments.
